claim: The no-in-degree-23 lemma is accepted. In a tournament on 52 vertices in which every triple has at least 5 dominators, no in-degree equals 23. A vertex of in-degree 24 need not exist: twenty-six in-degrees 25 and twenty-six in-degrees 26 already sum (in-degree minus 25) to 26. Whether or not an in-degree 24 occurs, some triple has at least 7 dominators. If every triple had at most 6 dominators, the sum of C(|D(Y)|, 2) would equal 5 times the sum of |D(Y)| minus 331500, while the common-out-neighbour count is at least 1158 larger. Erdős problem 902 is not solved.
definitions: T is a tournament on 52 vertices in which every triple has at least 5 dominators. D(X) is the set of vertices outside X that beat every vertex of X. e(v) = d^-(v) - 25, so the handshaking lemma gives sum_v e(v) = 26. Z is the set of vertices with d^-(v) = 24, and z = |Z|. A pair P is tight when |D(P)| = 11. For the no-in-degree-23 argument, v is a vertex of in-degree 23, A = N^-(v), B = N^+(v), R_a = D({a, v}) for a in A, and A_b = A intersect N^-(b) for b in B. (SF) is the structural fact in proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md section 3: if a dominator u of a tight pair has in-degree 25, then every outside vertex that beats u meets the dominator set in exactly 5 vertices. Claim Q is Lemma 2.3 of proof/ERDOS902_PROOF.md: z is at most 5. J(P) is the sum of e over D(P). The cubic weight used below is f(e) = 5e^3 - 177e^2. k(Y) = |D(Y)| for a triple Y. Erdős problem 902 asks for the order of f(n); this report does not determine it.
argument:
Verdict on the lemma. The counting in proof/N52_ATTEMPT.md section 2 does not have a failing step. The introduction of proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md is not used: that file stops during section 3, and section 3 is used only for (SF).

Step 1 holds at order 52. The in-degree of a in T[A] equals |D({a, v})|, which is at least 11 because every triple through {a, v} supplies the pair bound. These 23 in-degrees sum to C(23, 2) = 253 = 23*11, so each equals 11, T[A] is 11-regular, and every pair {a, v} is tight with dominator set R_a = A intersect N^-(a). Every vertex of A has out-degree 11 in A, so it lies in the dominator set of a tight pair and Lemma T gives e at least 0 on A.

Step 2 holds. Summing the common in-neighbourhoods in A counts C(11, 2) at each of the 23 vertices, hence 23*55 = 1265. There are C(23, 2) = 253 pairs and 5*253 = 1265, so every pair in A has exactly 5 common in-neighbours in A. If u beats u' inside A, the other 21 vertices split into 5 common in-neighbours, 6 that beat u and lose to u', 5 that lose to u and beat u', and 5 common out-neighbours. Thus T[A] is doubly regular of order 23, and the blocks R_a are the blocks of the symmetric 2-(23, 11, 5) design.

Step 3 holds. A vertex a in A beats v and 11 vertices of A, so it beats d^+(a) - 12 = 14 - e(a) vertices of B. Each b in B has |A_b| = |D({v, b})| at least 11. The arc count is 23*14 - E = 322 - E on one side and at least 11*28 = 308 on the other, so E = sum_A e is at most 14. At least 23 - 14 = 9 vertices of A have e = 0.

Step 4 holds, using J at least 3 as the input already recorded for every tight pair under the triple hypothesis. For the tight pair {a, v}, the outside excess sums to 14 - J, hence to at most 11. A vertex b with A_b = R_a lies outside {a, v} union R_a and meets R_a in 11 vertices, contributing 6. Two such vertices would contribute 12, which is more than 11. At most one vertex of B meets A in a given block.

Step 5 holds, and this is the step that uses (SF). Fix r in A with e(r) = 0 and b in B with b beating r. For each of the 11 vertices a in A that r beats, r lies in R_a. The vertex b lies outside {a, v} union R_a, so (SF) says that b meets R_a in exactly 5 vertices. Summing those 11 intersections gives 55. The same sum equals the sum, over x in A_b, of the number of common out-neighbours of r and x in A. Since b beats r, r is not in A_b, and every other pair in A has 5 common out-neighbours, so 55 = 5|A_b| and |A_b| = 11. For every a in A, |A_b intersect R_a| equals |D({v, a, b})|, which is at least 5. The 23 numbers x_a = |A_b intersect R_a| - 5 are therefore nonnegative. Each point of A lies in 11 blocks, so the sum of the intersection sizes is 11*11 = 121 and the sum of the x_a is 121 - 5*23 = 6. Each pair of points lies in 5 blocks, so the sum of n_a(n_a - 1) is 11*10*5 = 550. Then the sum of x_a^2 is 550 + 121 - 10*121 + 25*23 = 36, equal to 6^2. For nonnegative numbers the cross terms in (sum x_a)^2 vanish only when a single x_a equals 6. That block is all of A_b. The corresponding vertex a_b does not have r as an in-neighbour in A, so a_b lies in the 12-vertex set {r} union N^-_A(r).

Step 6 holds. The vertex r has in-degree 25, of which 11 lie in A, and r beats v, so r has 14 in-neighbours in B. Each produces a block, and distinct vertices of B produce distinct blocks. Fourteen vertices cannot land in a 12-vertex set. No in-degree equals 23.

Degree 24 is not forced. With every in-degree at least 24 one has e(v) at least -1, and Claim Q gives z at most 5, but z = 0 is compatible with the degree sum: twenty-six zeros and twenty-six ones sum to 26. The case distinction transported from order 51, where the sum of e is 0, does not force a negative part at order 52.

The restriction. Some triple has at least 7 dominators. The proof covers z = 0 and every z from 1 to 5 by the same comparison.

Two identities. For any two vertices u and v, |N^+(u) intersect N^+(v)| = |D({u, v})| + 1 - e(u) - e(v). Summing over the C(52, 2) = 1326 pairs, each e(w) appears 51 times, and 51*26 = 1326, so the common-out sizes have the same sum as the pair-dominator sizes. Lemma S1 supplies that common sum: sum_P |D(P)| = 16237 + (1/2) sum e(v)^2. Write S for the sum of squares and Q for the sum of cubes. Both are integers and S is even, because e^2 and e have the same parity and the sum of e is even. Under e(v) at least -1, e(v) at most 26, and z at most 5, the largest S is 706, from in-degrees 51, 30, five 24s and the rest 25s. The sum of the common-out sizes is then at most 16237 + 353 = 16590, which lies strictly between 12*1326 = 15912 and 13*1326 = 17238. The sum of C(c, 3) over 1326 nonnegative integers of sum m is minimized when the integers differ by at most 1, and the minimum on this range is L = 313170 + 33S. The excess over twelve on each pair is r = 325 + S/2, and L = 1326*C(12, 3) + 66r.

The triple sum T = sum_Y k(Y) equals sum_v C(26 - e(v), 3). For every integer e at most 26 the binomial coefficient equals the cubic (26 - e)(25 - e)(24 - e)/6 = (15600 - 1874e + 75e^2 - e^3)/6. Summing over 52 vertices and using sum e = 26 gives 6T = 762476 + 75S - Q. If every triple had k(Y) in {5, 6}, the identity C(5, 2) = 10 and C(6, 2) = 15 would give sum_Y C(k(Y), 2) = 5T - 15*C(52, 3) = 5T - 331500. The same sum equals the sum of C(|N^+(w) intersect N^+(w')|, 3) over unordered pairs, which is at least L. The difference is (55640 - 177S + 5Q)/6 = (55640 + sum_v f(e(v)))/6.

Minimum of the weight. It is enough to show that sum f is at least -48692, since (55640 - 48692)/6 = 1158. The value f(0) is 0 and f(-1) = -182. For a fixed z, the remaining 52 - z vertices have nonnegative excess summing to M = 26 + z, and M is at most 31. The sum of f on those vertices is minimized by a partition of M into positive parts, as follows. For positive integers a and b, f(a + b) - f(a) - f(b) = 3ab(5(a + b) - 118). A part of size at least 24 can be replaced by its two nearest halves, both at least 12, and the weight drops. Two positive parts whose sum is at most 23 can be merged, and the weight drops. An optimal partition therefore has every part at most 23 and every two parts summing to at least 24. Three such parts would sum to at least 36, which is larger than M. The optimal partition has exactly two positive parts: a single part M is at least 26 and splits into two parts with a drop in weight. For the two-part sums g(k) = f(k) + f(M - k), the forward difference is g(k + 1) - g(k) = delta(k) - delta(M - k - 1), where delta(e) = f(e + 1) - f(e) = 15e^2 - 339e - 172. If L = M - k - 1 is greater than k, then delta(L) - delta(k) = (L - k)(15(L + k) - 339). Along the path toward equal parts one has L + k = M - 1 at least 25, so the second factor is at least 375 - 339 = 36. Every forward step toward the centre decreases g. The minimum is the split floor(M/2) + ceil(M/2), together with z copies of f(-1) and the remaining zeros.

The six minima are positive. For z = 0 the parts are 13 + 13. f(13) = 169*(65 - 177) = -18928, the weight is -37856, and the difference is (55640 - 37856)/6 = 2964. The in-degrees are two 38s and fifty 25s. For z = 1 the parts are 13 + 14. f(14) = 196*(70 - 177) = -20972, the weight is -39900 - 182 = -40082, and the difference is 2593. For z = 2 the weight is 2*f(14) + 2*f(-1) = -42308 and the difference is 2222. For z = 3, f(15) = 225*(75 - 177) = -22950, the weight is -43922 - 546 = -44468, and the difference is 1862. For z = 4 the weight is 2*f(15) + 4*f(-1) = -46628 and the difference is 1502. For z = 5 the parts are 15 + 16. f(16) = 256*(80 - 177) = -24832, the weight is -47782 - 910 = -48692, and the difference is (55640 - 48692)/6 = 1158. The in-degrees are five 24s, forty-five 25s, one 40 and one 41.

The smallest of these six numbers is 1158. Every other admissible score sequence has larger weight, because any other partition of its positive excess moves away from the split above or uses a smaller z, both of which increase the difference. Therefore sum_Y C(k(Y), 2) is at least 5T - 331500 + 1158 whenever the score sequence is admissible. The assumption that every triple has at most 6 dominators makes the two sides equal to 5T - 331500. Some triple has at least 7 dominators, both when z = 0 and when z is positive.

The balanced sequence used in proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md section 7 is the case S = Q = 26 inside the same formula. Its difference is (55640 + 26*f(1))/6 = (55640 - 4472)/6 = 8528, and 8528 = 314028 - 305500, the two numbers printed there. That sequence is the maximum of the weight, not the minimum. The bound 1158 is what remains after the unbalanced sequences are included.

Direct check of the extreme. For five vertices of excess -1, forty-five of excess 0, one of excess 15 and one of excess 16, S = 486 and Q = 7466. The out-degrees contribute T = 5*C(27, 3) + 45*C(26, 3) + C(11, 3) + C(10, 3) = 14625 + 117000 + 165 + 120 = 131910. Then 5T - 331500 = 328050. The common-out sum is 16237 + 243 = 16480 = 12*1326 + 568, so L = 758*220 + 568*286 = 329208. The gap is 329208 - 328050 = 1158.

This does not produce a vertex of in-degree 24, it does not exclude a tight pair, and it does not show that an S_4 tournament on 52 vertices is impossible. Erdős problem 902 is not solved.

steps.1: 253 = 23*11, so T[A] is 11-regular and every {a, v} is tight; Lemma T gives e >= 0 on A
steps.3: 322 - E >= 308, so E <= 14 and at least 9 vertices of A have e = 0
steps.4: one block copy contributes 6, and 14 - J <= 11, so 12 > 11
steps.5: (SF) gives eleven intersections equal to 5; 55 = 5|A_b|; sum x = 6 and sum x^2 = 36
steps.6: 14 in-neighbours in B land in a 12-vertex set

evidence.sf_source: proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md section 3 only; the introduction of that file is not used

weaknesses: The status proved covers the acceptance of the no-in-degree-23 count and the uniform 7-dominator bound. Step 4 of that count uses J >= 3. That bound is the argument in research/AGENT_TASKS/R1-G-audit-every-n.report.json, used here as an input and not rewritten. (SF) is taken from the completed proof in section 3 of proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md; the introduction of that file claims several later theorems, and those claims are not evidence because the file stops during section 3. Claim Q is an input: the comparison uses z <= 5, and it does not use the stronger sentence that each vertex of Z has at most two in-neighbours in Z. The same arithmetic still forces a 7-dominator triple for every z <= 8, and the formal difference becomes negative at z = 9, so the appeal to Claim Q has room, but without some upper bound on z the comparison does not close. The convex lower bound L uses only the sum of the common-out sizes. Extra constraints can only raise the sum of C(c, 3), so they do not weaken the contradiction, and 1158 is not asserted to be the gap of a realized tournament. No tournament was enumerated, Landau's condition was not needed, and the J = 3, 4 tree was not reopened. A tight pair at order 52 remains possible. Erdős problem 902 is not solved, and f(4) is not evaluated.
next_step: Keep the minimum in-degree at 24 and keep both score regimes, z = 0 and z > 0. The slack 1158 is smallest on five in-degrees 24, forty-five in-degrees 25, one in-degree 40 and one in-degree 41; the next counting should test that sequence, and the balanced sequence, against a triple whose dominator count is at least 7. Do not treat an in-degree 24 as known to exist, and do not reopen the J = 3, 4 tree.
relation_to_prior: f(4) >= 52 is settled and is not reopened. The order-51 reduction is not repeated: at order 51 the sum of e is 0, while at order 52 it is 26, so the absence of in-degree 24 is the balanced possibility twenty-six 25s and twenty-six 26s rather than a regular tournament. The no-in-degree-23 count in proof/N52_ATTEMPT.md section 2 is accepted, with (SF) taken from section 3 of proof/swarm/r1_AUDIT-52-B.md. proof/N52_TIGHT_PAIRS.md section 7 already forces a triple with at least 7 dominators when every in-degree is 25 or 26, and it stops there. The bound here is the same second-moment comparison with that balanced hypothesis removed, so it applies when an in-degree 24 is present and when none is present. J >= 3 is an input from the every-order audit and is not re-proved. The J = 3 and J = 4 tree is not rebuilt. The exhausted approach keys are not used.
novelty: The new statement is the single lower bound of 1158 on L - (5T - 331500), valid for every score sequence with in-degrees at least 24 and at most five in-degrees equal to 24. It forces some triple to have at least 7 dominators in both regimes. The printed section 7 records only the balanced value 8528, which is the maximum of this weight, attained at twenty-six 25s and twenty-six 26s. The exchange that pins the minimum at the two-part split of 26 + z, and the six gaps 2964, 2593, 2222, 1862, 1502 and 1158, are not in the existing notes.
